To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) dynamic changes in blood flow and acoustic attenuation are necessary to accurately predict the extent of thermal ablation; (2) thermal dose (t43), thermal damage (Ω) and temperature (54–50°C) are all suitable for monitoring the extent of thermal damage in tissue during ablation; and (3) thermal dose and thermal damage measures are suitable for treatment planning purposes.

accounting for dynamic acoustic attenuation is critical for accurate prediction of ablation zone size and thermal damage indicators are good surrogates for temperature for treatment planning, while temperature thresholds may provide a cheaper surrogate for feedback control during the ablation.

accounting for dynamic changes in tissue properties is critical for predicting the extent of ultrasound ablation, and that thermal dose and thermal damage indicators are in good agreement with temperature-based ablation zones for this modality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and validating a theoretical model of ultrasound heating and thermal ablation in biological tissues.
the development of a theoretical model for ultrasound-based ablation, which is capable of predicting the extent and the shape of the ablation zones for different heating durations and temperatures.
the theoretical aspects of the feedback control of thermal ablation using catheter-based ultrasound sources, and the implications for the treatment planning, monitoring, and control of this modality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dynamic changes in blood flow, acoustic attenuation, and temperature-dependent tissue properties should be incorporated into models of thermal ablation.

the inclusion of dynamic changes in blood flow and acoustic attenuation is important in the modelling of thermal ablations, and that the use of thermal dose (t43) is recommended for monitoring and control of ablations with this technology.

the inclusion of dynamic changes in blood flow and attenuation/absorption in the modelling of thermal ablations with ultrasound is important, but that temperature-based feedback control is not significantly impacted by the inclusion of these effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the inclusion of dynamic changes in tissue acoustic properties and perfusion in models of ultrasound ablation is important, and that thermal dose and Arrhenuis damage are the most appropriate indicators of thermal damage for monitoring ablations with ultrasound.
dynamic models of blood perfusion and attenuation are not necessary for accurate predictions of thermal ablation zones for typical 5–10 min treatments with this modality.
the inclusion of dynamic changes in tissue properties during heating is essential for accurate treatment planning and monitoring with this modality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
for feedback controlled ultrasound ablation, it is important to consider dynamic changes in blood flow, acoustic properties, and thermal dose when modelling ablation extents.

the impact of dynamic changes in tissue properties during heating should be included in the model when performing treatment planning or monitoring of ultrasound ablation, particularly for short-duration treatments.
dynamic changes in tissue acoustic properties during heating should be accounted for in thermal ablation planning and monitoring.
